posts.title: Vinyl records continue making a comeback, improving the economics of local record shops
posts.description: Record Parlor of Muncie is located inside the Rose Court building in downtown Muncie.  (Daniel Huber / IPR News) Derrick McNelly is the owner of Record Parlor of Muncie. He’s located downtown and is one of five record stores in East Central Indiana. When he opened his shop about a year and a half ago, he said he started with 300 records, but now, he has around 4,000. “Honestly, the community is where it was at, and it still is. I hardly ever have to go seeking out inventory when it comes to used records at this point; people bring them to me,” McNelly said. A new record usually brings him $5 to $7 in profit, whereas those used records bring in anywhere between $7 and $20 each. The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) reported that in 2025, vinyl records generated over $1 billion in revenue. posts.title: Science Behind the Forecast: How you shop on Black Friday can affect the climate
posts.description: Black Friday is the biggest shopping day of the year (Erik Mclean / Unsplash) This week on Science Behind the Forecast, we’ll learn how Black Friday shopping can affect the weather. LPM’s Bill Burton talks about the effects with meteorologist Tawana Andrew. This segment originally aired in November 2019. It’s been edited for clarity and length. Tawana Andrew: It is Black Friday, so we're ready to shop, right? Bill Burton: Bring on the deals! Weather can actually affect how and where we shop, right? TA: Exactly. And in turn, where and how we shop can affect the weather, so that's something to keep in mind. USPS, the United States Postal Service, says that between Thanksgiving Day and New Year's Day, it's expected to make around 800 million deliveries. That's a lot of packages, and of course, the weather influences what we shop for. Warmer temperatures lasting into the winter can mean a lower demand for coats for certain stores. posts.title: Eco groups claim Louisville air pollution regulator mishandled permits for LG&E
posts.description: Coal stacks at Mill Creek Generating Station (Ryan Van Velzer / LPM) Two environmental groups argue a city air regulator broke federal law when it recently greenlit permits for Louisville Gas & Electric Co. to build a pair of natural-gas electricity-making units at the utility’s Mill Creek Generating Station in southwest Jefferson County. The Kentucky Resources Council and the Sierra Club filed a petition in October that asks the Louisville Metro Air Pollution Control Board to “set aside,” or cancel, the permits. The board has oversight of the Air Pollution Control District and its permitting decisions. Byron Gary, senior attorney for the Kentucky Resources Council, said if the board grants their request, it could reinstate a requirement that LG&E close a coal-powered generator as the first new natural gas unit comes online — which is expected next summer.
